Page numbers are from the Behringer *X32 Preliminary User Manual* (see Works Cited). The manual covers firmware 2.x,
so newer firmware may add things it doesn't mention.

## Electric guitar into the X32

### Why not plug it straight in?

The 32 inputs on the back are **mic preamps**. Their input impedance is **10 kΩ** balanced (p. 69), and the six
**Aux In** jacks are 20/40 kΩ line inputs. A passive guitar pickup wants a load many times higher than that. On a 10 kΩ input its treble
goes, its level drops, and it sounds thin and dull. **The X32 has no instrument (Hi‑Z) input.**

**Use a DI box.** It takes the guitar's high‑impedance signal and sends a balanced mic‑level signal down an XLR cable
into a preamp. This is the same as plugging in a mic. Pedals can go between the guitar and the DI.

```{=html}
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Guitar</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b opt">Pedals<small>optional</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b">DI box<small>¼″ in, XLR out</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b">Snake / XLR input</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">X32 channel<small>gain, EQ, comp</small></div>
</div>
```

Active DIs need phantom power (+48 V on that channel) or a battery. Passive DIs need neither.

### Three ways to get a tone

```{=html}
<p class="chain-label">1 · Clean, on the desk alone</p>
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Guitar → DI</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Channel EQ + compressor</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">FX send: reverb / delay / chorus</div>
</div>
<p class="chain-label">2 · The X32's own amp simulator</p>
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Guitar → DI</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Channel insert<small>FX slot set to “Insert”</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Guitar Amp<small>SansAmp‑style, cab sim</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">EQ, sends</div>
</div>
<p class="chain-label">3 · An amp modeller in front of the desk</p>
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Guitar</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b">Modeller<small>Helix, Tonex, Boss GT…</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b">XLR / line out</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">X32 channel</div>
</div>
```

1. **Clean.** The guitar goes through a DI with channel EQ and compression, plus some reverb on an FX send. It
   works for clean jazz, funk and acoustic‑style parts, but gives no distortion.
2. **The built‑in amp.** The effects rack has a **Stereo / Dual Guitar Amp** "modeled after the Tech 21 SansAmp",
   which "allows an electric guitar player to sound great without using an amp on stage" (p. 25). Its controls are
   Preamp, Buzz, Punch, Crunch, Drive, Low, High and Level, and a **Cabinet** simulation you can switch off. There is
   also a **Tube Stage** for milder overdrive. To use it:
   1. Choose an empty FX slot. Slots 5–8 can only be inserts (p. 19).
   2. In the FX screen, set the slot's source to **Insert** and load **Dual Guitar Amp**. The "Dual" version is two
      mono amps, so one slot can serve two guitars.
   3. Select the guitar channel. On its **Config** page, use the 6th encoder to pick the insert, for example
      **Ins FX5L**, then press the encoder to connect it (p. 31).
3. **A modeller.** A floor modeller or amp‑in‑a‑pedal does the amp and cabinet itself and sends a finished tone into
   the desk. Most have an XLR or balanced line output, so they need no DI. Turn off the modeller's cab sim only if a
   real cabinet is also being miked.

With a real amp on stage, you can still mic the amp's speaker (an SM57 close to the cone), take a DI split before
the amp, or both.

## Processed vocals

### What the desk does

```{=html}
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Mic</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Gain<small>+48 V for condensers</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Low cut</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Gate</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">EQ</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Compressor</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk opt">Insert<small>de‑esser, pitch</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">FX sends<small>reverb, delay</small></div>
</div>
```

Every channel has a **gate, a compressor and a parametric EQ**. See [gates](../lessons/live-gate.qmd),
[EQ](../lessons/live-eq.qmd) and [compression](../lessons/live-comp.qmd). The effects rack (60 effects, p. 60)
holds most vocal effects:

| Effect | X32 effect | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Reverb | Hall, Plate, Rich Plate, Room, Chamber, Vintage… | On an **FX send**, so several voices share it |
| Echo / slapback | Stereo Delay, 3‑Tap Delay, Rhythm Delay | On an FX send, timed to the song by tapping the tempo |
| Doubling | **Dual / Stereo Pitch** with a few cents of detune and a short delay (p. 25) | Insert, or a send for a subtle effect |
| Octave up or down | Dual / Stereo Pitch (±1 octave), Suboctaver | Insert. Fixed interval only |
| Taming "s" sounds | **Dual / Stereo DeEsser** | Insert |
| Warmth / grit | Tube Stage, Exciter, Enhancer | Insert, used lightly |
| Radio / telephone voice | Channel EQ: cut below ~400 Hz and above ~3 kHz | No effect slot needed |

### What the desk can't do

The manual lists no **pitch correction (Auto‑Tune)**, no **harmoniser** that follows the key, and no
**vocoder**. The pitch shifter moves the voice by a fixed interval, so a harmony a third above goes out of key
on some notes. For these, add one of:

- **A vocal processor** (for example a TC‑Helicon VoiceLive) between the mic and the desk, or on the channel's
  insert through an Aux Out and Aux In.
- **The computer** (next section).

## A Windows computer with Ableton

### The X‑USB card

The standard expansion card in the X32 is the **X‑USB**: one USB 2.0 cable carries **32 channels each way**
between the desk and a computer, at 44.1 or 48 kHz, 24‑bit (p. 37–42). It also does MIDI and DAW control
(Mackie Control / HUI).

**Windows:** install the **X32 ASIO driver** from behringer.com (run `Setup.exe`, p. 40). In Ableton, go to
**Options → Preferences → Audio**, then choose Driver Type **ASIO** and the X‑USB device, and turn on the input
and output channels you need. **Mac:** no driver is needed (Core Audio).

```{=html}
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b desk">X32 inputs 1–32</div><div class="a">⇄</div>
  <div class="b desk">X‑USB card<small>32 × 32, USB 2.0</small></div><div class="a">⇄</div>
  <div class="b pc">Windows PC<small>X32 ASIO driver</small></div><div class="a">⇄</div>
  <div class="b pc">Ableton Live</div>
</div>
```

On the desk, two routing screens set what goes where:

- **Routing → Card Out** chooses what goes *to* the computer, in banks of 8. **Local 1–8** sends the preamps on
  channels 1–8 (p. 54).
- **Routing → Home** chooses what each channel *listens to*, again in banks of 8: the local preamps or **Card
  1–8 … 25–32**, which are the computer's outputs (p. 54). Aux In 1–4 can also take Card 1–4 (p. 52).

### Four things to do with it

**1. Record every channel.** Set Card Out to Local 1–32. In Ableton, arm a track per input. A whole band is then
on separate tracks for mixing later. The desk's own USB‑stick recorder only makes a **stereo** 16‑bit WAV
(p. 36), so use the card for multitrack.

**2. Virtual soundcheck.** Record the band once. Afterwards, switch Routing → Home to the **Card** banks and play
the recording back through the same channels to practise the mix with no band in the room. When a channel listens
to the card, its gain knob becomes a ±12 dB trim (p. 39). Save two scenes, **"preamps"** and **"DAW"**, so the
switch is one recall (p. 39). This is a good way for students to practise the [sound check](../lessons/live-soundcheck.qmd).

**3. Ableton as an effects rack.** Send a channel to the computer, process it in Ableton, and bring it back on a
spare channel:

```{=html}
<div class="chain">
  <div class="b">Guitar / vocal</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Ch 5 preamp</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Card Out 5</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b pc">Ableton track<small>input 5, monitor In</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b pc">Plug‑ins<small>amp sim, Auto‑Tune, vocoder</small></div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b pc">Output 25</div><div class="a">→</div>
  <div class="b desk">Ch 25<small>source Card 25–32</small></div>
</div>
```

Pull channel 5's fader down, or take it out of the mix, so you hear only the processed return on channel 25. In
Ableton, set the track's **Monitor** to **In**, its input to the X‑USB input, and its output to the return channel.
Possible plug‑ins:

- Guitar: Ableton's **Amp** and **Cabinet** (in Suite), Neural DSP, AmpliTube, Guitar Rig.
- Vocals: Auto‑Tune or other pitch correction, a harmoniser, Ableton's **Vocoder**.

**4. Backing tracks and a click.** Ableton plays stems out of separate card outputs into their own channels, so
each one has a fader. Send the **click** to an output that goes only to the drummer's monitor or in‑ear mix, never
to the main L/R.

### Latency: the catch

The desk itself is quick: input to output takes **0.8 ms** (p. 69). Going through the computer adds a round trip.
The manual gives **about 14 ms** for the X‑USB, "depending on system performance and application" (p. 42). A
performer hears their own voice or guitar late. Below about 10 ms most people don't notice, but past 15–20 ms it
feels like playing in an echo.

- In the X‑USB control panel (Settings) and in Ableton, set the **ASIO buffer** as low as the computer allows
  without clicks. Try 64, then 128 samples.
- Use few, light plug‑ins on the live tracks. Some amp sims and pitch correctors add a "lookahead" delay, so use
  their low‑latency mode.
- Recording, virtual soundcheck and backing tracks don't care about latency. Only *live processing that a performer
  hears* does.
- For the lowest delay on a guitar, use the X32's own Guitar Amp or a modeller pedal and keep the computer for
  recording.

## Quick reference

| I want… | Do this |
|---|---|
| A guitar into the desk | DI box → XLR input. Never a plain ¼″‑to‑XLR adapter |
| Distorted guitar with no amp | Insert the X32 **Guitar Amp** effect, or use a modeller pedal |
| A thicker vocal | Pitch effect with a few cents of detune (doubling), plus a plate reverb on a send |
| Auto‑Tune, a harmoniser or a vocoder | A vocal processor, or Ableton through the X‑USB card |
| To record the whole band | X‑USB card, Card Out = Local 1–32, a track per input in Ableton |
| To practise mixing with no band | Virtual soundcheck: Routing → Home → Card, or recall a "DAW" scene |

See also: [the UR22mkII interface](ur22mkii.qmd) for a smaller setup with one or two inputs.
